newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Senate approves Mexico-drugs measure.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Senate approves Mexico-drugs measure.

text.p: The Senate on Thursday approved legislation criticising Mexico's performance in the anti-drug war and listing goals for stepping up its efforts.

The measure was a compromise drafted in cooperation with the Clinton administration, which had opposed a House of Representatives vote last week to overturn President Bill Clinton's finding that Mexico has fully cooperated in fighting drugs.

Clinton ruled on February 28 that Mexico was a reliable ally in the war against drugs, a step required to spare it U.S. economic sanctions. Congressional critics insist Mexico did not merit such a declaration and the House voted to overturn it, suspending its rebuke for 90 days to give Mexico time to improve its record.

The House vote infuriated Mexico and the Senate agreed to a softer step, which has no practical effect but does criticize the Mexican anti-drugs effort as inadequate on several points and requires Clinton to report by September 1 on progress by the U.S. and Mexican governments to improve matters.

The Senate measure, approved by a vote of 94-5, requires progress on dismantling drug trafficking organizations, on strengthening bilateral cooperation and border enforcement and on denying safe havens to traffickers.

The report would have to detail actions on crop eradication, money laundering and criminal screening of law enforcement officers. It calls for information on progress by the United States in anti-drug education, international drug interdiction and deployment of 1,000 additional immigration patrol agents.
